hood_desc: The postcard canal district of flower-draped half-timbered houses, best explored by a short boat ride or a stroll along the Lauch river.
The pedestrianized medieval core with the largest church and most shops and restaurants; the natural base for any visit.

The blocks around Colmar station, a ten-minute walk west of the old town, where most of the chain and mid-priced hotels sit and where you land if you arrive by train from Strasbourg or Basel. Plainer than the centre, but everything is still walkable.

food.desc: Sauerkraut slow-cooked in Riesling with juniper, buried under smoked pork, ham hock and several sausages. Meant for winter and for sharing.

places.name: Winstub Le Flory

food.name: Baeckeoffe
food.desc: Three meats and potatoes marinated overnight in white wine, sealed in a clay pot with a bread-dough ring and baked for hours. Order it a day ahead.

places.name: Wistub Brenner
places.note: Reliably good baeckeoffe brought to the table in its glazed terrine.

places.name: La Maison Rouge

food.name: Tarte flambee
food.desc: Flammekueche: paper-thin dough spread with fromage blanc, cream, onion and bacon, blasted in a wood oven. Ordered in rounds, one after another.

places.name: Wistub Brenner

places.name: Rue des Tanneurs winstubs

food.name: Fleischschnacka
food.desc: Snail-shaped spirals of fresh pasta rolled around braised beef, sliced and pan-fried, then served in broth or with salad. A true Colmar-area dish.

places.name: Winstub Le Flory
places.note: One of the few places keeping fleischschnacka on the regular menu.

places.name: Wistub Brenner

places.name: Rue des Tanneurs winstubs

food.name: Coq au Riesling
food.desc: Chicken braised in dry Alsatian Riesling with mushrooms and cream, served with buttered spaetzle. The region's answer to Burgundy's coq au vin.

places.name: La Maison Rouge
places.note: Classic creamy version with house spaetzle; solid value at lunch.

places.name: Wistub Brenner
places.note: Cooked with a named local Riesling; ask which grower is in the pot.

places.name: Winstub Le Flory
places.note: Cosy winstub setting for the wine-braised dishes on a cold evening.

food.name: Kougelhopf
food.desc: Tall fluted brioche studded with rum-soaked raisins and almonds, baked in a glazed earthenware mould. There is a savoury bacon and walnut version too.

places.name: Patisserie Gilg
places.note: The most talked-about bakery in Colmar and the easiest place to buy a good one.

places.name: Richon Patisserie Chocolaterie
places.note: Rated by many locals as the best kougelhopf in town, heavy on the rum.

places.name: La Patisserie des Tetes
places.note: Refined kouglofs and cakes in the landmark Maison des Tetes building.

food.name: Alsace white wine
food.desc: Colmar is capital of the Alsace wine road: dry Riesling, spicy Gewurztraminer, rich Pinot Gris and light Pinot Blanc, all in tall green flutes.

places.name: Domaine Karcher
places.note: A working family winery inside the city with tastings in its old courtyard.

places.name: L'Un des Sens
places.note: Chef-run wine cellar and bar, now one of Colmar's essential tasting stops.

places.name: Maison des Vins d'Alsace
places.note: Regional wine body's home; good orientation to the seven grapes and the grands crus.

food.name: Cremant d'Alsace and eaux-de-vie
food.desc: Traditional-method sparkling wine made all along the wine road, plus crystal-clear fruit brandies distilled from pear, plum, raspberry and quetsch.

places.name: Domaine Karcher
places.note: Pours its own cremant alongside the still wines in the tasting room.

landmarks: La Petite Venise (Little Venice)
Colmar's most enchanting quarter lines the Lauch canal with flower-decked half-timbered houses, best admired from the Saint-Pierre bridge or a flat-bottomed boat.
Musée Unterlinden
Housed in a 13th-century convent, this world-class museum guards Grünewald's shattering Isenheim Altarpiece, one of Western art's supreme masterpieces.
Maison Pfister
Built in 1537 for a wealthy hatter, this frescoed, wooden-galleried Renaissance house with corner oriel is the very emblem of old Colmar.
Collégiale Saint-Martin
Colmar's great Gothic collegiate church, often called a cathedral, raises its distinctive glazed-tile Mongol-style spire above the old town's main square.
Maison des Têtes (House of Heads)
A flamboyant 1609 Renaissance mansion studded with 106 carved grimacing heads, crowned by a Bartholdi statue of an Alsatian cooper.
Musée Bartholdi
The birthplace of Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, sculptor of the Statue of Liberty, displays his models, drawings, and the story of Liberty's creation.
Koïfhus (Old Custom House)
Colmar's oldest public building, a 1480 customs hall with a glazed green-and-yellow tiled roof, once seat of the Décapole league of Alsatian cities.
Quai de la Poissonnerie (Fishmonger's Quay)
The rainbow-painted fishermen's cottages along this canal-side lane form Colmar's most photographed row, gateway between the Krutenau and Little Venice.
Église des Dominicains (Dominican Church)
This soaring 14th-century Gothic hall church enshrines Martin Schongauer's exquisite Madonna of the Rose Bower, a jewel of late-medieval Rhenish painting.
Marché Couvert (Covered Market)
A handsome 1865 brick-and-iron market hall on the Lauch canal, brimming with Alsatian cheeses, charcuterie, kougelhopf, and oyster bars.

train.note: Colmar station is a ten-minute walk west of the old town and lies on the Strasbourg-Mulhouse-Basel main line, so cross-border trains are frequent rather than occasional - around 19 direct services a day reach Basel SBB in about 45-60 minutes. Strasbourg is 30 minutes away and Paris Gare de l'Est about 2h40m by direct TGV. Germany is reached by changing at Mulhouse or Strasbourg, or by taking the cross-border bus to Breisach and picking up the local train to Freiburg. Basel has three stations - make sure your ticket says Basel SBB, as the German-run Basel Bad Bf is a separate terminus on the other side of the city.

intl.to: Breisach am Rhein (Germany) - cross-border local line

bus.note: FlixBus and the other long-distance coaches use the stop at Place de la Gare on Rue Georges Lasch, right by the railway station, and around 64 destinations are reachable directly. The cheapest way into Germany is the cross-border Fluo Grand Est bus to Breisach, which takes 30-40 minutes and costs only a few euros, with an onward train to Freiburg. International coach tickets are online or app purchases; regional Fluo tickets can be bought from the driver. All these crossings are within Schengen, but ID is still worth carrying for spot checks on the Rhine bridges.

ferry.note: Colmar is inland in the Alsace plain and has no ferry service. The flat-bottomed boats in the Petite Venise quarter are 30-minute sightseeing trips on the Lauch, not transport, and run mainly from March to December. Rhine river cruise ships call at Breisach, about 25 km east across the German border.

half.name: Riquewihr
half.blurb: A walled medieval wine village on the Alsace Wine Route, its cobbled lanes lined with half-timbered houses.

half.name: Eguisheim
half.blurb: A circular fortified village of flower-decked half-timbered houses, considered one of the birthplaces of Alsatian wine.

notes.walk: The compact old town is entirely walkable and one of the best-preserved in France; a car is useful for the surrounding Alsace Wine Route villages
notes.card: Widely accepted; cash useful for small market stalls
notes.safety: Very safe town, popular with visitors of all ages. Petty theft in crowded market season is the main concern.
notes.religion: Roman Catholic (majority); Protestant (notable Alsatian minority); no religious affiliation (growing minority)
notes.langs: French; Alsatian (regional dialect, still spoken by some); German (widely understood due to proximity)
notes.net: Strong 4G/5G coverage citywide. Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes. ~€10-20 for a 10-20GB prepaid tourist SIM. Free wifi widely available. An Orange, SFR, or Bouygues tourist SIM or eSIM.
notes.transit: Trace Colmar Agglomération urban bus network
notes.transport: Basel-Mulhouse-Freiburg EuroAirport (BSL/MLH), about 45 min away; Strasbourg Airport is a further alternative. Direct TGV/TER rail connections to Strasbourg (35 min) and Paris (under 3 hr). Regional buses connect to Alsace Wine Route villages. Well connected via the A35 motorway; the old town is best explored on foot.
